task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought: Hi! How can I help you today?
turns.execution_output: User: Hello... yes, hi. I'm having a bit of trouble with my phone. For the past few hours I can't send picture messages — you know, the ones with photos of my grandchildren. It just won't go through. I'm John Smith, by the way. Can you help me?

turns.thought: Of course, I can help you with that picture messaging issue. To pull up your account, could you please confirm your **date of birth** (YYYY-MM-DD) and the **phone number** for the line you're having trouble with?
turns.execution_output: User: My phone number is 555-123-2002. As for my date of birth... oh dear, I'm not sure I have that written down anywhere handy. Could you maybe look me up with my name and number instead? I'm John Smith. I do apologize, I'm not very good with all this.

turns.thought: Let me check your account for anything that could affect service.

turns.thought:
Thanks for confirming, Mr. Smith. I was able to pull up your account using your phone number — no need to worry about the date of birth.

Here's what I can see so far:
- **Line 555-123-2002** is **Active** (not suspended)
- Your account is in good standing — no overdue bills
- Data usage is 8.7 GB out of 15 GB, so you haven't hit your data limit

So the problem is most likely a setting on your phone. Let's check a few things together, one step at a time.

**First, could you look at the very top of your phone screen (the status bar) and tell me what icons or symbols you see up there?** For example, do you see an airplane symbol, signal bars, "5G"/"4G"/"LTE", a Wi-Fi symbol, or something like "No Signal"?
turns.execution_output: User: Let me take a look at the top of my screen for you.

turns.thought:
Not bad at all — nothing is broken, and you certainly didn't do anything wrong! Airplane Mode is a setting on every phone that turns off all the wireless connections — cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth. It's very easy to switch on by accident, sometimes just by brushing the screen or a button press while the phone is in a pocket or bag. That's almost certainly why your picture messages won't send — the phone can't reach the network at all while it's on.

Here's how to turn it off:

1. **Swipe down from the very top of the screen** with one finger (start at the top edge and pull downward). This opens your quick settings panel.
2. Look for the **airplane symbol** — it's usually a small airplane icon, and it will probably be highlighted/colored in (that means it's ON).
3. **Tap that airplane icon once** to turn it OFF. It should turn grey or dim.
4. Wait about 10–20 seconds. You should then see the signal bars and something like "5G" or "LTE" appear at the top of the screen.

Once you've done that, could you tell me **what you now see at the top of your screen** — the signal bars and any network letters (like 5G, LTE, or 4G)? Then we'll test whether your picture messages are working again.

You haven't broken anything — no need to worry. "No Signal" just means the phone hasn't reconnected to the network yet, and "Data Disabled" is a separate switch that also needs to be turned on. Both are normal to see right after coming out of Airplane Mode, and both are easy to fix.

Let's tackle them one at a time.

**Step 1 — Turn Mobile Data back on:**
1. Open the **Settings** app (the gear icon on your home screen).
2. Tap **"Network & Internet"** — on some phones it's called **"Connections"** or **"Mobile Network."**
3. Tap **"Mobile network"** (or "SIMs").
4. You should see an option called **"Mobile data"** with a switch next to it. **Tap the switch so it turns on** (it will usually slide to the right and turn blue or green).

Once that's on, look at the top of your screen again.

**Could you tell me what you see now — does it still say "No Signal," or do you see signal bars and something like 5G, LTE, or 4G?**

If it still says "No Signal" after a minute or so, we'll try a couple of other simple things next — I'll walk you through those. Nothing you've done so far has caused any harm.

Please don't worry — **your photos are completely safe.** Nothing that's happened so far can delete pictures from your phone. When a picture message fails to send, it simply stays in your messaging app as an unsent draft, and the photo itself remains in your gallery. You haven't lost anything.

You're not doing anything wrong either — the steps you've taken were exactly right.

Since the screen still says "Data Disabled" even though the switch is on, the phone may just need a fresh start to get everything talking to the network again. Let's try that.

**Step 1 — Turn Mobile Data off and back on (this "wakes up" the switch):**
1. Go back to **Settings → Network & Internet → Mobile network** (or "Connections → Mobile Network").
2. Tap the **"Mobile data"** switch to turn it **OFF**.
3. Wait about **10 seconds**.
4. Tap it again to turn it **ON**.

**Step 2 — Restart the phone:**
1. Press and hold the **power button** (the button on the side or top of the phone) for a few seconds.
2. A menu should appear — tap **"Restart"** (or "Reboot"). If you only see "Power off," tap that instead, wait 30 seconds, then press the power button again to turn the phone back on.
3. Once the phone has fully started up, **wait about one minute**, then look at the top of the screen.

When it comes back on, could you tell me **exactly what you see at the top of the screen** — signal bars, "No Signal," "Data Disabled," "Data Enabled," or something like 5G/LTE/4G?

Whatever it says, we'll take the next step from there. We're making progress — Airplane Mode is off and Mobile Data is on, which were the two big things.

I completely understand your concern — those photos are precious, and I want to be very clear and reassuring with you.

**Yes, I'm quite sure it's safe.** A restart is one of the most routine things you can do with a phone, and here's why your photos are protected:

- **A restart does not erase anything.** It doesn't touch your photos, your messages, your contacts, or your apps. It simply turns the phone's software off and then on again, like turning a light switch off and on — the furniture in the room stays exactly where it is.
- **Your pictures live in your phone's storage** (and often also in a cloud backup). A restart never wipes storage. The only things that erase a phone are a "factory reset" or "erase all content" — and **I will never ask you to do that.**
- **The only important precaution:** a restart works best when the phone has battery remaining. Yours is at **80%**, which is plentiful. Nothing to worry about there.

**One extra reassurance you might like:** if your photos are also saved to a service like Google Photos or iCloud, they exist in two places at once. But it's entirely optional to check that — it's not needed for the restart to be safe.

So here's all you need to do:

1. Press and hold the **power button** for a few seconds.
2. Tap **"Restart"** (or "Power off," then turn it back on after 30 seconds).
3. Wait about a minute after it starts up.

Whenever you're ready, go ahead. And when the phone is back on, tell me **exactly what you see at the top of the screen** — any signal bars, "No Signal," "Data Disabled," or something like 5G/LTE/4G — and we'll go from there. There's no rush at all.
turns.execution_output: User: Well... alright. You sound very sure, and I do trust you. Let me do it.

turns.thought:
I'm so glad your photos are safe — that's the most important thing. I completely understand the frustration; you've been doing everything right and nothing has changed, which is genuinely annoying. Let's keep going — we're not out of options.

**The reassuring news:** "No Signal" is a very common and very fixable problem. It just means the phone isn't "talking" to the network at the moment. It has nothing to do with your photos or anything stored on the phone.

**Before we continue, I confirmed on your account:**
- Your line (555-123-2002) is **Active** — not suspended
- Your bills are **up to date** — nothing overdue
- You've used 8.7 GB of your 15 GB data allowance, so you have **plenty of data left**

So this isn't a problem with your account or service — it's a settings/hardware connection issue on the phone itself. That's good news, because those we can usually fix.

**Here's the next thing to try — checking the SIM card.** The SIM is the tiny card that identifies your phone to the network. If it's slightly loose, the phone shows "No Signal" even when everything else is correct.

1. **Turn the phone off completely** (press and hold the power button, then tap "Power off").
2. Find the **small pinhole** on the edge of the phone. Look in the box your phone came in for a small metal tool shaped like a paperclip — or a plain paperclip works fine.
3. **Gently push** the tool into the pinhole until the little tray pops out slightly.
4. **Pull the tray all the way out.** You'll see the tiny SIM card sitting in it.
5. Check it looks seated flat and clean, then **push the tray firmly back in** until it clicks flush with the phone.
6. **Turn the phone back on** and wait about one minute.

Then tell me what you see at the top of the screen.

**One note:** some newer phones don't use a physical card at all — they use a built-in "eSIM." If you open the tray and **there's no card in it**, don't worry at all — just push the tray back in, turn the phone on, and tell me "no SIM card in the tray." I'll take you down a different path instead.

And if at any point you'd rather have a person walk you through this on the phone instead, just say the word and I'll connect you with one of my colleagues — no pressure either way.
turns.execution_output: User: I don't think I can be poking around inside my phone with a paperclip — I'd be terrified of breaking something. Is there anything else we can try first, something simpler? I'm sorry to be difficult.

turns.thought:
I'm so sorry — please don't apologise, you're not being difficult at all. You've been wonderfully patient and you've done everything exactly right. Not wanting to poke around inside your phone is completely sensible, and I'd never want you to do something you're uncomfortable with.

Let me reassure you on two things I've checked on your account:

- **Your photos are safe.** Nothing we've done can touch them — and you've seen that for yourself after the restart. That worry can go away.
- **Your line and account are perfectly fine.** I confirmed your phone line (555-123-2002) is active, your bills are up to date, and you've plenty of data left (8.7 GB used of your 15 GB). So this is a connection problem on the phone itself, not anything to do with your service or payments.

There **is** one more gentle thing we can try — no poking, no tools:

**Try connecting to your home Wi-Fi.** Even without a cellular signal, picture messages can often travel over Wi-Fi instead. To do that:
1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **"Network & Internet"** (or "Connections"), then **"Wi-Fi."**
3. Make sure Wi-Fi is **ON**, then tap your home network's name from the list.
4. Enter your Wi-Fi password if asked (it's often on a sticker on your router, or on a card that came with your internet box).

Once you see the little Wi-Fi symbol at the top with your network name, try sending one of the photos again.

However — I want to be upfront with you rather than keep sending you in circles. The remaining fixes for "No Signal" do need a colleague of mine who can run deeper checks on your line and your phone from our end, including checking the network coverage in your area right now. You wouldn't need to do anything technical yourself — they'd handle it and talk you through it.

**Would you like me to connect you to one of my colleagues now?** I'll pass along everything we've already tried so you won't have to repeat yourself — including that we've confirmed Airplane Mode is off, Mobile Data is on, and the phone has been restarted.
turns.execution_output: User: Oh — wait. Before you transfer me, there's something I should probably mention. I'm not at home right now. I'm in France, visiting. I've been here a little while. Could that have something to do with it? I didn't think to say anything earlier, I'm sorry.

turns.thought:
Goodness — **that's very likely the whole explanation.** Thank you for mentioning it, and please don't apologise; it's genuinely useful information.

When you're abroad, your phone can't connect to our home network towers — it has to connect to a partner network over there instead. That's a feature called **roaming**, and it needs to be switched on for the phone to get a signal while you're in France. That's why you're seeing "No Signal."

I have good news — I've checked your line and **roaming is already enabled on your account**, so there's nothing to arrange and no charge to worry about on our side. We just need to switch it on in the phone's settings.

**Here's exactly what to do — no tools, no restarting needed:**

1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **"Network & Internet"** (it may be called **"Connections"** or **"Mobile Network"**).
3. Tap **"Mobile network"** (or "SIMs").
4. Look for **"Data roaming"** — sometimes it's labelled **"Roaming."**
5. **Tap the switch to turn it ON.** It will usually slide across and turn blue or green.
6. Your phone may show a small message asking if you're sure — tap **"OK"** or **"Enable."**

Then step away from the settings screen and **wait about a minute or two**. Your phone will search for a French network and connect to it.

**Then look at the top of your screen and tell me what you see** — you're hoping to see signal bars and something like 5G, LTE, 4G, or possibly the letter "R" (which stands for roaming). It may also show a French network name.

One other thing worth knowing: since you're in France on Wi-Fi at places like your hotel, picture messages can travel over that Wi-Fi too. So if turning roaming on doesn't immediately fix things, connecting to the hotel Wi-Fi is a good backup plan while we sort it out.

Will you give that roaming switch a try and let me know what the top of the screen says afterwards?
turns.execution_output: User: Oh, roaming! That makes sense, I suppose. Let me find that switch...

turns.thought:
You have every right to be frustrated — you've been patient and done everything I've asked, and we're still not there. I'm sorry it hasn't worked yet.

Before I hand you over, let me just double-check one thing on your account to make sure nothing has changed on our end.

I'm truly sorry it's come to this — you've been patient and diligent through every single step, and you have every right to be frustrated. You've done nothing wrong.

Let me tell you what I've confirmed on my end, so you know where things stand:

- Your line (555-123-2002) is **active** and in good standing
- Your bills are **up to date**
- You're using **8.7 GB of your 15 GB** allowance, so data isn't exhausted
- **International roaming is already enabled** on your account for France

So everything on your account and our network is correctly set up — yet you still have no signal. That means the remaining checks need to happen with tools only my colleagues have: they can run a live diagnostic on your line, check whether the French partner networks are currently accepting your phone, and look at your phone's SIM and network settings remotely. None of that requires anything technical from you at all, and they can walk you through it at your pace.

Let me connect you with one of them now. I'm passing along everything we've already tried, so you won't need to repeat a thing — Airplane Mode off, Mobile Data on, phone restarted, and Data Roaming now enabled — plus the fact that you're in France on an active, roaming-enabled line with photos you're trying to send.

YOU ARE BEING TRANSFERRED TO A HUMAN AGENT. PLEASE HOLD ON.

I'm sorry we couldn't quite get there together — you were very patient and did everything right. I've passed a full summary to my colleague so **you won't have to repeat yourself**. It includes that you're in France, that roaming is already enabled on your line, that your account and bills are all in good order, and every step we've already tried (Airplane Mode off, Mobile Data on, data toggled, phone restarted, roaming switched on).

One last reassurance before I hand you over: **your photos are safe.** Everything we tried — including the restart — cannot delete pictures from your phone.
